C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

noncomputable def inducition_with_necOnly! [H.HasNecOnly]
  {motive  : (φ : Formula α) → H ⊢! φ → Prop}
  (hMaxm   : ∀ {φ}, (h : φ ∈ H.axioms) → motive φ ⟨maxm h⟩)
  (hMdp    : ∀ {φ ψ}, {hpq : H ⊢! φ ➝ ψ} → {hp : H ⊢! φ} → motive (φ ➝ ψ) hpq → motive φ hp → motive ψ (hpq ⨀ hp))
  (hNec    : ∀ {φ}, {hp : H ⊢! φ} → (ihp : motive φ hp) → motive (□φ) (System.nec! hp))
  (hImply₁   : ∀ {φ ψ}, motive (φ ➝ ψ ➝ φ) $ ⟨imply₁ φ ψ⟩)
  (hImply₂   : ∀ {φ ψ χ}, motive ((φ ➝ ψ ➝ χ) ➝ (φ ➝ ψ) ➝ φ ➝ χ) $ ⟨imply₂ φ ψ χ⟩)
  (hElimContra : ∀ {φ ψ}, motive (Axioms.ElimContra φ ψ) $ ⟨ec φ ψ⟩)
  : ∀ {φ}, (d : H ⊢! φ) → motive φ d := by
  intro φ d;
  induction d using Deduction.inducition! with
  | hMaxm h => exact hMaxm h
  | hMdp ihpq ihp => exact hMdp (ihpq) (ihp);
  | hRules rl hrl hant ih =>
    rw [HasNecOnly.has_necessitation_only] at hrl;
    obtain ⟨φ, rfl⟩ := hrl;
    exact @hNec φ (hant (by simp)) $ ih (by simp);
  | hImply₁ => exact hImply₁
  | hImply₂ => exact hImply₂
  | hElimContra => exact hElimContra

same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

Conversely, suppose that the trivial theorem is derivable within the theory \( T \). This means there exists a proof within \( T \) for a statement that is trivially true, such as \( \top \). If \( T \) can derive a tautology, it demonstrates that \( T \) does not lead to contradictions, as deriving a tautology does not impose any new information or restrictions. Therefore, the ability to derive the trivial theorem implies that \( T \) is free from internal contradictions, thereby establishing its consistency.

**Conclusion:**

Since triviality (consistency) of a theory entails the derivability of its trivial theorem and vice versa, the two are, in fact, equivalent. Thus, a theory is trivial (consistent) if and only if its triviality is derivable within the theory.
